picks.title: Photoprotection comes at a cost: growth-productivity trade-offs associated with enhanced NPQ in Haematococcus lacustris.
picks.hook: Enhanced NPQ protects algae but cuts growth, revealing a trade‑off key to bloom dynamics.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to find out how boosting a protective mechanism called non‑photochemical quenching (NPQ) influences growth and astaxanthin production in the microalga Haematococcus lacustris.

The researchers grew cultures of H. lacustris under conditions that triggered different levels of NPQ and measured photosynthetic performance, stress‑induced differentiation, and overall productivity.

They observed that while higher NPQ helped dissipate excess light energy and shield the cells from photodamage, it also altered the balance between growth and stress tolerance, affecting astaxanthin accumulation.

Understanding this trade‑off is useful because it informs how we might balance light protection and biomass yield when cultivating algae for high‑value compounds.
picks.why: The findings help guide algae cultivation strategies to optimise both growth and valuable pigment production.

picks.title: Species- and reactor-aware machine learning for prediction and optimization of microalgal biomass productivity in photobioreactor-based bioresource systems.
picks.hook: Machine‑learning predicts microalgal yields across species and reactors, boosting photobioreactor design.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to improve the ability to predict how much biomass different microalgae can produce in photobioreactors, taking into account the specific algae species and the design of the reactor.

The researchers built a machine‑learning framework that incorporates information on the microalgal species, cultivation conditions, nutrient levels, and reactor geometry. They trained the model on data collected from a range of photobioreactor experiments.

The model was able to forecast volumetric biomass productivity and suggest optimal operating settings for each species‑reactor combination.

This approach could help streamline algae‑based bioprocesses by reducing trial‑and‑error experimentation.
picks.why: Accurate predictions can speed up algae cultivation, lowering costs for bio‑fuel and bioproduct production.

picks.title: Microalgal cell factories for bioenergy and climate action: a circular bioeconomy roadmap.
picks.hook: A roadmap shows how microalgal cell factories can power climate action and circular bio‑energy.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to map how microalgae could be used as tiny, fast‑growing factories that turn sunlight into renewable fuels and help cut greenhouse gases. 

The authors reviewed the characteristics of microalgae, noting their very high lipid (fat) content – often exceeding 70 % dry cell weight – and rapid growth rates, which together surpass those of traditional terrestrial crops. 

They evaluated the most advanced conversion pathways that turn algal biomass into biofuels such as biodiesel and other energy products, assessing the technical and environmental performance of each route. 

The review highlights that microalgae’s superior lipid yields and speed of cultivation make them a promising feedstock for diverse bioenergy applications. 

Understanding these pathways helps guide the development of a circular bioeconomy where algae‑derived fuels can contribute to climate mitigation.
picks.why: Microalgae’s high oil yield and fast growth could make algae‑based fuels a practical, low‑carbon energy source.

picks.title: Deciphering Melatonin-Driven Bioenergy Reprogramming Through Integrated Physiological and Metabolomic Analyses in Dunaliella salina.
picks.hook: Melatonin rewires Dunaliella metabolism, unlocking higher bio‑fuel potential.
picks.article: A recent study set out to explore how melatonin influences the way the micro‑alga Dunaliella salina allocates carbon and balances its internal redox state, with the aim of improving its usefulness as a renewable bio‑energy source. The researchers grew D. salina in a two‑stage cultivation system and added 20 µM melatonin during the first stage, then examined physiological responses and metabolite profiles to see how the hormone reshaped cellular metabolism. Their integrated analysis revealed that melatonin acts as a regulator of carbon flux allocation and redox homeostasis in the alga, indicating a shift in metabolic pathways that could affect biomass and lipid production. Understanding this hormonal control offers a potential route to boost algal bio‑energy yields.
picks.why: Melatonin‑driven metabolic tweaks could help produce more algal biomass or lipids for sustainable bio‑fuel.

picks.title: Programmable microalgae: Engineering sense-decide-adapt systems for dynamic environmental performance.
picks.hook: Engineered microalgae can sense, decide, and adapt to changing conditions for boosted industrial performance.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to give microalgae the ability to sense changing conditions, decide how to respond, and then adapt their metabolism accordingly. 

The researchers engineered microalgal strains with built‑in sensor circuits that detect environmental cues such as light, temperature, carbon dioxide, salinity and nutrient levels, and then trigger physiological changes. They tested these programmable cells under laboratory conditions that mimic the rapid shifts seen in industrial cultivation, ranging from seconds to seasonal timescales. 

The engineered algae were shown to integrate signals and adjust key pathways, including native nutrient‑sensing, photoprotective, carbon‑concentrating, and osmotic programs, demonstrating a functional sense‑decide‑adapt (SDA) system. 

This work points toward more resilient and efficient algal production platforms that can automatically optimise growth and product formation as conditions vary.
picks.why: Programmable algae could keep bioprocesses stable, reducing the need for constant manual control.

picks.title: Anti-inflammatory activity of Chlorella polysaccharide AHP.
picks.hook: A Chlorella polysaccharide shows strong anti‑inflammatory effects, hinting at new natural therapeutics.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether a polysaccharide extracted from the green micro‑alga Chlorella, called AHP, can calm inflammation linked to inflammatory bowel disease.

The researchers isolated the polysaccharide from Chlorella cells and tested it in laboratory models that mimic gut inflammation, looking at its ability to reduce inflammatory signals and to influence gut‑microbe balance.

The work showed that the Chlorella polysaccharide displayed anti‑inflammatory activity, immunomodulatory activity and the property of regulating gut microbiota, which could aid colon tissue repair and improve intestinal health.

These findings suggest that a natural product from algae might become a useful tool for managing gut inflammation.
picks.why: Algal polysaccharides like AHP could offer a natural way to support gut health and reduce inflammation.

picks.title: Quorum sensing molecules enhance cadmium detoxification and cellular removal in the marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum.
picks.hook: Quorum‑sensing molecules help the diatom Phaeodactylum detoxify cadmium, enhancing marine cleanup.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether bacterial quorum‑sensing molecules called cyl‑homoserine lactones (AHLs) can help a marine diatom, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, cope with cadmium, a toxic metal.

The researchers added exogenous AHLs to cultures of the diatom and monitored cell growth, metabolic changes, and how much cadmium the cells could remove.

They found that the AHLs influenced the diatom’s physiology and enhanced cadmium detoxification and cellular removal, although the abstract does not give specific quantitative results.

Understanding how these bacterial signals boost metal cleanup could inform new biotechnological approaches for treating polluted seawater.
picks.why: AHL‑enhanced diatoms may become a natural tool for cleaning cadmium‑contaminated marine environments.

picks.title: Study on the construction of algal-bacterial consortium comprising Pantoea vagans ZHS-1 and Nostoc sp. GD2 and its growth-promoting effect on rice.
picks.hook: A custom algal‑bacterial consortium boosts rice growth, offering a sustainable bio‑fertilizer route.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to build a partnership between a soil‑living bacterium and a nitrogen‑fixing cyanobacterium, then test whether this partnership could help rice grow better without chemical fertilizers.

The researchers combined the phosphate‑solubilizing bacterium Pantoea vagans ZHS‑1 with the nitrogen‑fixing cyanobacterium Nostoc sp. GD2 to form a consortium they called ZD‑1. The work was carried out in laboratory cultures where the two microbes were grown together and then applied to rice seedlings.

The study found that the ZD‑1 consortium promoted rice growth, indicating that the combined action of phosphorus release by the bacterium and nitrogen fixation by the cyanobacterium can enhance plant development.

This result is interesting because it shows a way to reduce reliance on synthetic fertilizers by using natural microbial allies to support crop productivity.
picks.why: Microbial consortia like ZD‑1 could help make rice farming greener by supplying essential nutrients naturally.

picks.title: CRISPR-Cas Tools for Dissecting and Engineering Environmental Responses in Microalgae.
picks.hook: CRISPR tools enable precise tweaking of microalgae to boost light and temperature resilience.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to develop CRISPR-Cas tools that allow precise genetic editing of microalgae, enabling researchers to understand and improve how these tiny photosynthetic organisms cope with changing light, temperature, nutrients and carbon dioxide.

The researchers applied CRISPR-associated proteins—molecular scissors guided by short RNA sequences—to microalgae cells, moving from random DNA insertion methods to targeted gene modifications. The work was carried out at the laboratory scale using standard molecular biology techniques.

They demonstrated that clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)‑Cas systems can be used to edit specific genes in microalgae, shifting the field from random transgene integration toward precise genome engineering.

This advancement is important because it opens the door to engineering algae that maintain high productivity under variable environmental conditions, which could benefit sustainable biofuel and bioproduct production.
picks.why: Precise gene editing can help create algae strains that grow well despite changing climates, boosting their use in biofuels and other green technologies.

picks.title: Alanine aminotransferase-acetyl-CoA carboxylase switching produces starch-rich bioethanol feedstock in Desmodesmus.
picks.hook: Switching key enzymes creates starch‑rich microalgae, a promising feedstock for bioethanol.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether tweaking two key enzymes could redirect carbon inside the tiny green alga Desmodesmus to make more starch, which can be turned into bioethanol. The researchers first altered the activity of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), an enzyme that links alanine and pyruvate, and then switched the function of acetyl‑CoA carboxylase (ACC), which normally drives lipid (fat) synthesis. They performed this sequential manipulation in nitrogen‑limited cultures of the strain Desmodesmus sp. CNW‑N, using a combination of physiological measurements, transcriptomics (gene‑expression profiling), enzyme assays, and inducible CRISPR‑based gene editing.

The integrated approach showed that the ALT‑mediated pathway and the ACC‑dependent lipid synthesis could be successfully re‑programmed, leading to a noticeable shift in how the cells allocated their internal carbon. The altered cells accumulated a higher proportion of starch while reducing lipid buildup, creating a feedstock richer in the carbohydrate needed for bioethanol production.

These findings demonstrate that precise enzyme switching can steer microalgal metabolism toward desired products, offering a potential route to more efficient, starch‑rich biofuel feedstocks.
picks.why: Redirecting carbon to starch in algae could make bioethanol production cheaper and more sustainable.

picks.title: Protective role of probiotics or Spirulina platensis supplementation against mercury-induced hematological, histopathological, and antioxidant-immune gene dysregulation in Nile Tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus).
picks.journal: Biometals : an international journal on the role of metal ions in biology, biochemistry, and medicine
picks.hook: Spirulina or probiotics shield fish from mercury toxicity, preserving blood and immune genes.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether adding beneficial bacteria (probiotics) or the blue‑green algae Spirulina platensis to the diet of Nile tilapia could lessen the harmful effects of mercury exposure.

The researchers fed groups of tilapia either a probiotic mix containing Bacillus subtilis, Lactobacillus plantarum and L. buchneri, or a diet supplemented with Spirulina, then exposed the fish to mercury and examined blood parameters, tissue structure and the activity of antioxidant and immune‑related genes.

The results showed that both the probiotic regimen and the Spirulina supplement provided protection against mercury‑induced disruptions in blood chemistry, tissue damage and the dysregulation of antioxidant‑immune genes.

These findings suggest that natural dietary additives could help safeguard farmed fish from heavy‑metal stress, supporting healthier aquaculture production.
picks.why: Probiotic or Spirulina feeds may protect farmed fish from mercury, improving safety and sustainability in aquaculture.

picks.title: Bacterial contamination control in Chlorella sorokiniana cultivation using NVC-H antimicrobial peptide.
picks.hook: An antimicrobial peptide curbs bacterial contamination, stabilizing large‑scale Chlorella growth.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether a synthetic antimicrobial peptide called NVC‑H could keep bacterial contamination under control in large‑scale cultures of the green microalga Chlorella sorokiniana.

The researchers added the NVC‑H peptide to Chlorella sorokiniana cultures and monitored its effect on bacterial growth. The work was done at a scale relevant to commercial microalgal production and tested both Gram‑positive and Gram‑negative bacterial strains.

The peptide displayed antibacterial activity against both Gram‑positive and Gram‑negative bacteria, with inhibition that varied depending on the bacterial strain.

Keeping bacterial contamination in check is important for maintaining high algal biomass yields and stable processing conditions.
picks.why: Effective bacterial control can boost algae biomass production, making algal bioproducts more reliable and affordable.

picks.title: Biogas production and biomolecule degradation from Chlorella vulgaris using a lagoon-digester granular sludge versus a silty sludge adapted to microalgae.
picks.hook: Chlorella vulgaris yields biogas efficiently in lagoon vs. silty sludge, revealing a greener waste-to-energy route.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to compare how well two different types of sludge—granular sludge taken from an industrial lagoon digester and a silty sludge that had been adapted to microalgae—could turn Chlorella vulgaris biomass into biogas and break down its biomolecules.

The researchers fed the same amount of Chlorella vulgaris into two laboratory reactors, each inoculated with one of the sludge types, and monitored gas production and the degradation of biomolecules over time.

They reported the first evaluation of biogas output and biomolecule degradation kinetics using the spontaneously formed granular sludge from the lagoon digester, showing how this sludge performed with the algal feedstock.

The work highlights that granular sludge from existing lagoon systems may be a viable inoculum for converting algal waste into renewable energy, offering a potentially more efficient route for algae‑based biorefineries.
picks.why: It suggests a new way to boost biogas yields from algae, helping turn waste into renewable fuel.

picks.title: Matrix matters: the importance of the food matrix in bioaccessibility and basolateral recovery of microalgal-sourced DHA.
picks.hook: The food matrix dramatically boosts DHA absorption from microalgal oil, reshaping omega‑3 nutrition.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see how the food matrix – the other ingredients surrounding a nutrient – influences how much DHA from microalgae becomes available for absorption and how much reaches the bloodstream.

The researchers compared DHA delivered in a typical encapsulated oil (a triglyceride form) with DHA incorporated into a more complex food matrix, using in‑vitro digestion models that simulate the human gastrointestinal tract.

They found that the matrix‑based delivery improved the bioaccessibility of DHA and increased its basolateral recovery, meaning more of the fatty acid was available for uptake after digestion.

Understanding how the surrounding food components affect DHA uptake can help design more effective algae‑derived nutritional products.
picks.why: Better matrix design could boost the health benefits of algae‑based DHA supplements.

picks.title: The genomic origins of cyanobacterial morphological diversity.
picks.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
picks.hook: Genomic analysis uncovers the evolutionary roots of cyanobacterial shape diversity.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to uncover the genetic basis for the wide range of shapes and structures seen in cyanobacteria, the only prokaryotes that perform oxygenic photosynthesis.

The researchers examined the genomes of cyanobacterial species that display diverse forms, from filamentous chains to cells that differentiate into specialized types, looking for patterns that could explain how these organisms switch between single‑cell and multicellular lifestyles.

They found that the genomic mechanisms driving the repeated transitions between unicellularity and multicellularity remain unresolved, indicating that the genetic switches behind these morphological changes are still unknown.

Understanding these hidden genetic controls is interesting because it could eventually inform how we engineer cyanobacteria for biotechnological applications.
picks.why: Deciphering cyanobacterial shape control may help tailor algae for sustainable bio‑production.

picks.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled real-time monitoring of intracellular lipid dynamics in microalgae via optical sensors and kinetic early-warning differentiation.
picks.hook: AI‑driven optical sensors track intracellular lipid drops in real time, warning of stress before it hits.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to develop a way to watch the tiny lipid droplets that microalgae make in real time, without harming the cells. The researchers built an artificial‑intelligence‑driven sensing system that watches colour changes over time (chron‑spectral colour evolution) in a microalgal photobioreactor.

They used optical sensors to capture the colour signals from the algae and applied AI algorithms to interpret those signals, allowing non‑invasive, real‑time monitoring and early‑warning detection of lipid droplet dynamics.

The study demonstrated that this AI‑enabled system could continuously track intracellular lipid droplet synthesis and provide early warnings of changes in lipid production.

This capability could help optimise microalgae cultivation for bio‑fuel and other high‑value lipid products.
picks.why: Real‑time, non‑invasive lipid monitoring can improve algae‑based bio‑fuel production efficiency.

picks.title: Species- and reactor-aware machine learning for prediction and optimization of microalgal biomass productivity in photobioreactor-based bioresource systems.
picks.hook: Machine learning predicts and boosts microalgal biomass in photobioreactors, tailoring species and reactor settings.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to improve how we predict and boost the growth of microalgae in photobioreactors, taking into account the specific algae species and the design of the reactor. The researchers built a machine‑learning framework that incorporates information about the algae, cultivation conditions, nutrients, and reactor geometry. Using data from multiple species grown in different reactor setups, the model was trained to forecast volumetric biomass productivity and to suggest optimal operating parameters.

The model was able to predict productivity across the tested conditions and identified key factors that drive higher yields. By tailoring the predictions to each species and reactor type, the approach offers a way to fine‑tune cultivation without extensive trial‑and‑error experiments.

This work is interesting because it provides a data‑driven tool that could make algae‑based bioprocesses more efficient and scalable.
picks.why: Species‑specific, reactor‑aware predictions can streamline algae cultivation, lowering costs for biofuel and bioproduct production.

picks.title: Biomimetic Mineralized Capsules for Haematococcus pluvialis Clustering and Functional Regulation.
picks.hook: Biomimetic capsules cluster Haematococcus pluvialis, enhancing astaxanthin production for nutraceutical use.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to help the green microalga Haematococcus pluvialis, a valuable source of the antioxidant astaxanthin, grow more efficiently by protecting the cells from environmental and mechanical stress.

The researchers created biomimetic mineralized capsules that mimic natural protective structures and encapsulated the algae within a hydrogel matrix. The approach was tested at a laboratory scale using standard culturing conditions.

The work showed that the mineralized capsules enabled clustering of H. pluvialis cells and provided functional regulation that reduced their susceptibility to stress, while still allowing the algae to produce astaxanthin.

These findings are interesting because they suggest a way to improve microalgal production of high‑value compounds without relying on complex genetic or process controls.
picks.why: Encapsulating algae in protective capsules could boost astaxanthin yields, making sustainable production more reliable.

picks.title: Microalgal cell factories for bioenergy and climate action: a circular bioeconomy roadmap.
picks.hook: Roadmap outlines microalgal cell factories as a circular platform for renewable energy and carbon mitigation.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to map how microalgae could be used as versatile microbial cell factories for renewable energy and climate‑change mitigation. The authors highlighted that many microalgal strains contain very high lipid content, often exceeding 70 % dry cell weight, and grow much faster than traditional terrestrial crops, making them attractive feedstocks for diverse bioenergy applications.

The review examined advanced conversion pathways that turn algal biomass into fuels such as biodiesel and other biofuels. It evaluated the technical performance of these pathways, focusing on how the high lipid yields and rapid growth translate into efficient fuel production.

The authors concluded that microalgae’s superior lipid accumulation and growth rates give them a clear advantage over conventional crops for bioenergy, positioning them as a key component of a circular bioeconomy that supports climate action.

Understanding these advantages helps guide research and investment toward algae‑based technologies that could supply cleaner fuels while reducing greenhouse‑gas emissions.
picks.why: Algae’s high oil yield and fast growth make them a promising, sustainable source for cleaner biofuels.

picks.title: Multifunctional Potential of Bacillus vallismortis C-305 for Cyanobacterial Bloom Suppression: Algicidal Activity, Organic Matter Transformation, and Plant Stress Mitigation.
picks.hook: Bacillus vallismortis strain curbs harmful cyanobacterial blooms while improving water quality and plant health.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether a naturally occurring bacterium could help keep harmful algal blooms, especially those caused by Microcystis aeruginosa, in check. The researchers isolated a strain of Bacillus vallismortis called C-305 and tested its ability to act as an algicidal agent.

They grew the bacterial strain in the laboratory and exposed cultures of the cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa to it, observing any inhibitory effects. The work was carried out at a scale typical for controlled lab experiments.

The study found that Bacillus vallismortis C-305 was highly efficient at suppressing the growth of Microcystis aeruginosa, demonstrating strong algicidal activity.

These results suggest that this bacterial strain could become a useful tool for environmentally friendly management of harmful algal blooms, offering an alternative to chemical or physical control methods.
picks.why: A potent, natural bacterial ally could help protect water bodies and irrigation safety from toxic algae.

picks.title: Species- and reactor-aware machine learning for prediction and optimization of microalgal biomass productivity in photobioreactor-based bioresource systems.
picks.hook: Machine‑learning predicts microalgal biomass yields across species and reactor designs.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to improve the way we predict how much microalgal biomass can be produced in photobioreactors, taking into account the specific algae species and the design of the reactor.

The researchers built a machine‑learning framework that incorporates data on microalgal species, cultivation conditions, nutrients, and reactor design, and they applied it to volumetric productivity predictions.

The model was able to predict and optimise biomass productivity by considering both species‑specific traits and reactor characteristics, enabling more accurate forecasts of how much algae can be grown under given conditions.

This approach could help streamline algae‑based bioprocesses by tailoring cultivation strategies to the right species and reactor setup.
picks.why: Accurate, species‑aware predictions can speed up algae bioproduct development and lower production costs.

picks.title: Anti-inflammatory activity of Chlorella polysaccharide AHP.
picks.hook: Chlorella polysaccharide AHP shows strong anti‑inflammatory effects in vitro.
picks.article:
A recent study examined whether a polysaccharide extracted from the green micro‑alga Chlorella, called AHP, can calm inflammation in the gut. The researchers tested the compound’s ability to reduce inflammatory signals and to modulate the gut microbiome, which together influence colon health.

The work used purified AHP polysaccharide in laboratory experiments that measured anti‑inflammatory activity and immunomodulatory effects. The scale of the tests was limited to in‑vitro assays, focusing on how the substance interacts with immune cells and microbial communities.

The findings confirmed that the Chlorella polysaccharide displayed anti‑inflammatory activity and immunomodulatory activity, and it also helped regulate gut microbes, suggesting it could aid colon tissue repair and improve intestinal health.

These results are interesting because they point to a natural algal product that might be developed into a supplement or therapeutic ingredient for supporting gut health.
picks.why: Algal polysaccharides like AHP could become gentle, plant‑based tools for easing gut inflammation and supporting a balanced microbiome.

picks.title: Quorum sensing molecules enhance cadmium detoxification and cellular removal in the marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum.
picks.hook: Quorum‑sensing molecules boost cadmium removal by the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether bacterial quorum‑sensing molecules called cyl‑homoserine lactones (AHLs) could help a marine diatom, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, cope with cadmium, a toxic metal.

The researchers added exogenous AHLs to cultures of the diatom and monitored cell growth, metabolic changes and the amount of cadmium removed from the medium.

They found that the AHLs influenced the diatom’s physiology and enhanced cadmium detoxification and cellular removal, although the abstract does not give exact quantitative details.

These results suggest that microbial communication signals could be harnessed to improve metal‑cleaning capabilities of microalgae.
picks.why: Using bacterial signaling molecules may boost algae’s ability to clean heavy metals from seawater.

picks.title: Biomimetic Mineralized Capsules for Haematococcus pluvialis Clustering and Functional Regulation.
picks.hook: Mineralized capsules cluster Haematococcus pluvialis, enhancing astaxanthin production.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to help the micro‑alga Haematococcus pluvialis, a valuable source of the antioxidant astaxanthin, grow more reliably by shielding it from environmental and mechanical stress. The researchers created tiny capsules that mimic natural mineral shells and used them to cluster the algae cells together. They tested the capsules on Haematococcus pluvialis cultures, observing how the mineralized shells affected cell growth and stress tolerance.

The method involved encapsulating the algae in biomimetic mineral layers, forming clusters that could be handled more easily. The work was carried out at a laboratory scale using standard culturing techniques.

The study found that the mineralized capsules provided protection to the algae, reducing susceptibility to environmental and mechanical stress while allowing controlled growth conditions.

These findings are interesting because they suggest a way to improve the consistency and efficiency of astaxanthin production from micro‑algae, which could benefit both the nutraceutical and aquaculture industries.
picks.why: Mineral capsules could make algae‑based astaxanthin production more reliable and scalable.

picks.title: Biomimetic Mineralized Capsules for Haematococcus pluvialis Clustering and Functional Regulation.
picks.hook: Mineralized capsules boost Haematococcus clustering, enhancing astaxanthin yields.
picks.article:
A recent study aimed to develop a way to cluster the green microalga Haematococcus pluvialis and control its growth and stress responses using biomimetic mineralized capsules.

The researchers used hydrogel encapsulation to surround the algal cells, creating mineralized capsules that mimic natural protective structures. The work focused on the algae’s production of astaxanthin, a valuable ketocarotenoid with antioxidant activity.

The study showed that hydrogel encapsulation offers a protective environment for the cells, helping to manage growth and stress conditions that normally affect free‑living cells.

Such a strategy could make it easier to produce astaxanthin more reliably, which is important for nutraceutical and other applications.
picks.why: Encapsulating Haematococcus pluvialis could boost steady astaxanthin production for health and industry.

picks.title: Quorum sensing molecules enhance cadmium detoxification and cellular removal in the marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum.
picks.hook: Quorum‑sensing molecules help diatoms strip cadmium from marine water.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether bacterial quorum‑sensing molecules called cyl‑homoserine lactones (AHLs) can help a marine diatom, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, cope with cadmium, a toxic metal.

The researchers added exogenous AHLs to cultures of the diatom and measured cell growth, metabolic changes and how much cadmium the cells could remove.

They found that the AHLs influenced the diatom’s physiology and enhanced cadmium detoxification and cellular removal, although the abstract does not give specific numbers.

These results suggest that microbial communication signals could be harnessed to improve metal cleanup using algae.
picks.why: AHL‑boosted diatoms may offer a greener way to strip toxic cadmium from seawater.

picks.title: Molecular Evaluation of Deep Eutectic Solvents for Wet Algae Lipid Extraction and Biofuel Production.
picks.hook: Deep eutectic solvents efficiently pull lipids from wet algae for fuel.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether environmentally friendly liquids called deep eutectic solvents (DES) and certain ionic liquids could help break open micro‑algae cells and release their oil for biofuel.

The researchers tested four chlorine‑based ionic liquids and several DES formulations on the wet micro‑alga Chlorella vulgaris, measuring how well each pretreatment freed lipids without drying the biomass.

They identified a geranic acid‑based DES (CG 1‑2 DES) as the optimal agent for promoting lipid release under wet conditions.

Finding a green pretreatment that works on wet algae could simplify the step of extracting oil, a known bottleneck in scaling algae‑based biofuels.
picks.why: A greener, wet‑process pretreatment could lower costs and energy use in algae biofuel production.

picks.title: Influence of microplastics on microalgal performance during wastewater polishing.
picks.hook: Microplastics impair microalgal wastewater polishing performance.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see how common microplastics influence the performance of microalgae used to polish wastewater. The researchers focused on five types of plastic particles that are frequently detected in wastewater streams.

They grew microalgal cultures in laboratory‑scale wastewater treatment setups and added each of the five plastics – polypropylene, polystyrene, polyamide, low‑density polyethylene and another polymer – to assess any changes in algal growth or activity.

The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results, only noting that the effects of these microplastics on the algae were evaluated.

Understanding whether microplastics hinder algae‑based wastewater treatment is important for designing resilient and effective water‑cleaning technologies.
picks.why: If microplastics impair algae, treatment plants may need new strategies to maintain clean water.

picks.title: Biogas production and biomolecule degradation from Chlorella vulgaris using a lagoon-digester granular sludge versus a silty sludge adapted to microalgae.
picks.hook: Chlorella vulgaris yields biogas efficiently in lagoon digester versus silty sludge.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see how well a granular sludge taken from an industrial lagoon digester could turn the micro‑alga Chlorella vulgaris into biogas and break down its biomolecules, and to compare that performance with a silty sludge that had been adapted to micro‑algae.

The researchers fed Chlorella vulgaris biomass to two types of anaerobic (oxygen‑free) digester sludge – a spontaneously formed granular sludge from a lagoon digester and a silty sludge pre‑adapted to algae – and measured biogas output and the rates at which the algal biomolecules were degraded.

The study provides the first evaluation of biogas production and biomolecule degradation kinetics using the lagoon‑digester granular sludge with Chlorella vulgaris as substrate.

These findings are useful because they help identify which type of sludge might be more effective for converting algal waste into renewable energy.
picks.why: Understanding sludge performance guides more efficient algae‑based biogas production for sustainable energy.

picks.title: Microalgal cell factories for bioenergy and climate action: a circular bioeconomy roadmap.
picks.hook: Roadmap outlines microalgal cell factories for renewable energy and carbon mitigation.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to map how microalgae could be used as tiny, fast‑growing factories that turn sunlight into renewable energy and help curb climate change. The authors reviewed the high lipid content—often exceeding 70 % dry cell weight—of many microalgal species and their rapid growth rates, comparing them with traditional land crops.

They examined the latest conversion pathways that turn algal biomass into biofuels such as biodiesel and other energy products, assessing the technical and economic feasibility of each route.

The review found that microalgae’s lipid yields and growth speed significantly surpass those of conventional terrestrial crops, making them a promising feedstock for diverse bio‑energy applications.

Understanding these advantages helps guide the development of a circular bioeconomy where algae‑based processes can provide sustainable fuels and contribute to climate mitigation.
picks.why: Microalgae’s high oil yields and fast growth make them a strong candidate for sustainable biofuel production.

picks.title: Extremophilic Microalgae and Cyanobacteria as Platforms for Climate Resilience, Circular Resource Utilization and Bioprospecting.
picks.hook: Extremophilic microalgae and cyanobacteria offer robust platforms for circular resource use.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to explore how the untapped genetic diversity of extremophilic microalgae and cyanobacteria could help meet several Sustainable Development Goals, including clean water, affordable energy and land‑based livelihoods. 

The authors reviewed existing literature on these hardy microorganisms, focusing on the range of species, their mechanisms for coping with extreme conditions, and the biotechnological possibilities they present. 

They found that extremophilic microalgae and cyanobacteria possess distinct physiological and biochemical traits that make them promising platforms for climate‑resilient applications, circular resource use and bioprospecting. 

The review highlights how these organisms could be leveraged for resource recovery and other sustainable technologies, underscoring their potential role in future environmental solutions.
picks.why: Their unique traits could enable algae‑based processes for clean water, renewable energy and land‑based sustainability.

picks.title: Protective role of probiotics or Spirulina platensis supplementation against mercury-induced hematological, histopathological, and antioxidant-immune gene dysregulation in Nile Tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus).
picks.journal: Biometals : an international journal on the role of metal ions in biology, biochemistry, and medicine
picks.hook: Spirulina supplementation shields fish from mercury toxicity, restoring immune genes.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether adding common probiotics or the blue‑green alga Spirulina platensis to the diet of Nile tilapia could protect the fish from the harmful effects of mercury exposure. The researchers fed groups of tilapia either a probiotic mix (Bacillus subtilis, Lactobacillus plantarum, and L. buchneri) or Spirulina while exposing the fish to mercury, then examined blood parameters, tissue structure, and the activity of antioxidant and immune‑related genes.

The results showed that both probiotic and Spirulina supplementation reduced the mercury‑induced disruptions in blood cells, lessened tissue damage, and helped restore normal expression of antioxidant and immune genes compared with fish that received mercury alone.

These findings suggest that dietary probiotics or Spirulina can mitigate mercury toxicity in farmed fish, offering a practical strategy to improve fish health and food safety.
picks.why: Probiotic or Spirulina feeds could help keep farmed fish healthier in polluted waters, protecting both the aquaculture industry and consumers.

picks.title: Microalgal cell factories for bioenergy and climate action: a circular bioeconomy roadmap.
picks.hook: Roadmap shows microalgae cell factories powering renewable energy and carbon reduction.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to map how microalgae could be used as tiny, multifunctional factories for renewable energy and climate‑change mitigation. The authors highlighted that many microalgal species contain very high lipid (fat) levels, often exceeding 70 % of their dry cell weight, and grow much faster than traditional land crops, making them a promising feedstock for various bio‑energy products.

The review examined the latest advances in converting microalgal biomass into fuels such as biodiesel and other biofuels, focusing on the biochemical pathways that turn the algae’s abundant lipids into usable energy. It also considered how these processes fit into a circular bioeconomy, where waste streams are recycled and overall resource use is minimized.

The authors concluded that the combination of high lipid content and rapid growth gives microalgae a clear advantage over terrestrial crops for bio‑energy applications, and they evaluated the most advanced conversion routes currently available.

Understanding these advantages helps guide future research and development toward sustainable algae‑based fuels that could reduce reliance on fossil resources.
picks.why: High‑lipid, fast‑growing algae could become a key renewable fuel source, supporting greener energy and climate goals.

picks.title: Biogas production and biomolecule degradation from Chlorella vulgaris using a lagoon-digester granular sludge versus a silty sludge adapted to microalgae.
picks.hook: Chlorella vulgaris yields more biogas when digested with granular sludge versus silty sludge.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to compare how two different types of sludge – a granular sludge taken from an industrial lagoon digester and a silty sludge that had been adapted to microalgae – break down the biomass of the green alga Chlorella vulgaris and produce biogas.

The researchers fed Chlorella vulgaris biomass into anaerobic (oxygen‑free) digestion reactors that were seeded with either the spontaneously formed granular sludge or the silty microalgae‑adapted sludge. They then measured biogas output and tracked how quickly the algae’s biomolecules were degraded.

The work provides the first evaluation of biogas production and biomolecule degradation kinetics using the lagoon‑digester granular sludge with Chlorella vulgaris as the substrate.

Understanding which sludge type works best could help improve the efficiency of turning algal waste into renewable energy.
picks.why: It shows a path to more efficient algae‑based biogas, linking waste algae to renewable fuel production.

picks.title: Protective role of probiotics or Spirulina platensis supplementation against mercury-induced hematological, histopathological, and antioxidant-immune gene dysregulation in Nile Tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus).
picks.journal: Biometals : an international journal on the role of metal ions in biology, biochemistry, and medicine
picks.hook: Spirulina supplement shields against mercury toxicity, protecting blood and immune genes.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether giving Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) probiotic bacteria or Spirulina platensis could protect the fish from the harmful effects of mercury exposure. The researchers fed the fish diets supplemented with either a mix of Bacillus subtilis, Lactobacillus plantarum and L. buchneri, or with Spirulina, while exposing them to mercury and then examined blood parameters, tissue structure, and the activity of antioxidant and immune‑related genes.

The work measured changes in hematology (blood cell counts), histopathology (microscopic tissue damage) and the expression of genes involved in antioxidant defenses and immune responses. The results showed that both probiotic and Spirulina supplementation alleviated the mercury‑induced disturbances in these measures.

These findings suggest that natural dietary additives can help mitigate heavy‑metal stress in farmed fish, offering a potential strategy to improve fish health and food safety.
picks.why: Probiotic or Spirulina feeds could safeguard aquaculture species from mercury, supporting safer fish production.

picks.title: Near-infrared confocal imaging reveals the spatial organisation of far-red photosynthesis in Shark Bay microbial mats and Halomicronema sp.
picks.hook: Near‑infrared confocal imaging maps far‑red photosynthesis in Shark Bay microbial mats.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to map where far‑red photosynthesis occurs inside the layered microbial mats of Shark Bay, Australia, and to see how a filamentous cyanobacterium called Halomicronema sp. fits into that picture. The researchers used near‑infrared confocal microscopy, a technique that shines light of specific wavelengths and captures high‑resolution images from within a sample, to look at the mats at a microscopic scale. They found that far‑red light (wavelengths beyond the visible range) can penetrate the mat and support photosynthesis by the Halomicronema‑like filaments, which coexist with chlorophyll d/f‑containing phototrophs that absorb visible light. This spatial arrangement shows that far‑red photosynthesis is not limited to surface layers but extends deeper into the mat where visible light is depleted.

The work highlights how microbial communities can partition light resources, allowing different photosynthetic organisms to thrive side by side. Understanding this natural light‑sharing strategy could inform the design of engineered algal systems that make use of broader parts of the solar spectrum.
picks.why: It shows how algae can harvest far‑red light, suggesting ways to boost productivity in bio‑fuel or bioproduct cultures.

picks.title: Multifunctional Potential of Bacillus vallismortis C-305 for Cyanobacterial Bloom Suppression: Algicidal Activity, Organic Matter Transformation, and Plant Stress Mitigation.
picks.hook: Bacillus vallismortis C-305 curbs harmful cyanobacterial blooms while boosting plant stress resilience.
picks.article: A recent study set out to see whether a naturally occurring bacterium could curb harmful algal blooms caused by Microcystis aeruginosa, which threaten water quality and crop irrigation safety. The researchers isolated Bacillus vallismortis strain C‑305 and tested its ability to inhibit the algae in laboratory experiments. They found that the bacterium displayed strong algicidal activity against Microcystis aeruginosa, indicating it can suppress bloom formation. This suggests a promising, environmentally friendly tool for managing waterborne algal problems.
picks.why: Using a natural bacterial ally could help keep water bodies clear of toxic algae, protecting ecosystems and agriculture.

picks.title: Bacterial contamination control in Chlorella sorokiniana cultivation using NVC-H antimicrobial peptide.
picks.hook: Antimicrobial peptide NVC-H shields Chlorella sorokiniana farms from bacterial invaders, boosting yields.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether a synthetic antimicrobial peptide called NVC‑H could keep bacterial contamination under control in large‑scale cultures of the microalga Chlorella sorokiniana.

The researchers added the NVC‑H peptide to Chlorella sorokiniana cultivation systems and monitored its effect on bacterial growth. The peptide’s activity was tested against both Gram‑positive and Gram‑negative bacteria, which are the two broad classes of bacteria distinguished by differences in their cell‑wall structure.

The peptide proved to be antibacterial, inhibiting the growth of the tested bacteria. The degree of inhibition varied depending on the bacterial strain, indicating a strain‑dependent response.

Controlling bacterial contamination is important for maintaining high algal biomass yields and stable processing, making this approach potentially valuable for algal biotechnologies.
picks.why: Effective bacterial control can boost algae production efficiency, lowering costs for biofuels and nutraceuticals.

picks.title: Operational Regulation of Algal-Bacterial Granular Sludge for Nitrogen Removal Pathway Reconfiguration and N<sub>2</sub>O Mitigation.
picks.hook: Engineered algal‑bacterial granules cut N₂O emissions while efficiently removing nitrogen from wastewater.
picks.article:
A recent study explored how to steer the performance of algal‑bacterial granular sludge, a compact mixed community used for treating wastewater, so that it removes nitrogen more efficiently while producing less nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.

The researchers grew the granular sludge in a low‑hydraulic shear environment (0.5 cm s⁻¹) and systematically varied three operational parameters: the carbon‑to‑nitrogen (C/N) ratio, the light intensity, and the aeration rate.

By adjusting these conditions they were able to reconfigure the nitrogen transformation pathways within the granules and observed a corresponding impact on nitrous oxide emissions.

Understanding how to control these pathways could help make wastewater treatment greener and more effective.
picks.why: Optimizing algal‑bacterial granules can cut greenhouse‑gas emissions while improving nitrogen cleanup in wastewater.

picks.title: Banana pseudostem-derived hydrochar mitigates aluminum oxide nanoparticle toxicity to microalgae: implications for sustainable phosphate binder application in contaminated waters.
picks.journal: Journal of environmental science and health. Part A, Toxic/hazardous substances & environmental engineering
picks.hook: Banana‑stem hydrochar protects microalgae from aluminum oxide nanoparticle toxicity, enabling safer water treatment.
picks.article: A recent study explored whether a banana‑pseudostem derived hydrochar could reduce the harmful effects of aluminum oxide nanoparticles on harmless microalgae, which is important for using those nanoparticles as phosphate binders in polluted water. The researchers mixed the hydrochar with the aluminum oxide particles to create a composite material (HCA L) and then exposed a common microalgal species to the composite and to the nanoparticles alone. They measured algal growth and health indicators to see how the two treatments compared. The composite was found to lessen the toxicity of the aluminum oxide nanoparticles to the microalgae, indicating that the hydrochar can buffer the harmful impact. This suggests a way to make phosphate‑binding nanomaterials safer for the broader aquatic environment.
picks.why: Reducing nanoparticle toxicity helps keep algae healthy, supporting safer water treatment and ecosystem balance.

picks.title: Biomimetic Mineralized Capsules for Haematococcus pluvialis Clustering and Functional Regulation.
picks.hook: Biomimetic capsules boost Haematococcus clustering, enhancing astaxanthin yields for nutraceuticals.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to help the green microalga Haematococcus pluvialis, a valuable source of the antioxidant astaxanthin, grow more efficiently by clustering the cells and shielding them from stress. The researchers created biomimetic mineralized capsules – tiny, shell‑like structures that mimic natural minerals – and used them to encapsulate the algae. They tested how the capsules affected cell clustering and functional regulation under controlled laboratory conditions.

The encapsulation technique formed protective mineral shells around the algae, encouraging the cells to group together while reducing their exposure to environmental and mechanical stress. The study reports that the mineralized capsules provided a protective effect, though specific quantitative results are not given in the abstract.

These findings suggest a way to improve astaxanthin production by making Haematococcus cultures more robust and easier to manage, which could benefit both nutraceutical and aquaculture applications.
picks.why: Mineral capsules could boost algae resilience, helping produce more antioxidant pigment for food and health uses.

picks.title: Low-temperature plasma technology: comprehensive applications in microalgae cultivation, mutagenesis, and downstream processing.
picks.hook: Low‑temperature plasma improves microalgae growth, mutagenesis, and downstream processing in a single step.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to evaluate how low‑temperature plasma (LTP) technologies could improve the cultivation, genetic modification and downstream processing of microalgae. The authors reviewed dose‑dependent interactions between LTP and microalgae across the whole production chain, from growth in bioreactors to harvesting and product extraction.

They examined both atmospheric and room‑temperature plasma treatments, summarising experimental results reported in the literature. The review covered laboratory‑scale experiments where microalgae were exposed to plasma at varying intensities to assess effects on growth rates, mutation frequencies and cell wall disruption.

The analysis shows that LTP can enhance microalgal strain performance, induce useful mutations, and facilitate cheaper, more efficient cell disruption for product recovery. The authors highlight that plasma dosage is a key factor governing these outcomes.

These insights suggest that plasma‑based tools could become versatile, cost‑effective options for advancing algae‑based fuels, nutraceuticals and environmental applications.
picks.why: Plasma treatments may boost algae yields and simplify extraction, helping make algae products more affordable and sustainable.

picks.title: Predicting cyanotoxin concentrations in freshwater ecosystems: Bridging molecular indicators and explainable artificial intelligence.
picks.hook: AI links molecular markers to cyanotoxin levels, offering reliable forecasts for freshwater safety.
picks.article:
A recent study aimed to improve how we predict dangerous cyanotoxin levels in fresh‑water bodies by linking molecular signals to advanced artificial‑intelligence models.

The authors reviewed how genetic, physiological, ecological and hydrodynamic processes drive the link between algal biomass and toxin production, and they evaluated several modelling approaches for forecasting direct toxin concentrations.

The review highlighted three predictive strategies: forecasting bloom biomass, predicting toxin occurrence, and estimating threshold‑risk levels for toxin exposure.

Understanding which approach works best helps water managers anticipate toxin spikes more reliably, supporting safer drinking‑water supplies.
picks.why: Better toxin forecasts can protect drinking water and recreational lakes from harmful algal blooms.

picks.title: Extremophilic Microalgae and Cyanobacteria as Platforms for Climate Resilience, Circular Resource Utilization and Bioprospecting.
picks.hook: Extremophilic algae and cyanobacteria reveal traits for climate‑resilient bio‑resource platforms.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to explore how the untapped genetic diversity of extremophilic microalgae and cyanobacteria could help meet several Sustainable Development Goals, including clean water, affordable energy and land‑based livelihoods. 

The authors reviewed existing literature on these organisms, focusing on their diversity, the mechanisms they use to survive extreme conditions, and their biotechnological potential. No new experiments were performed; the work is a synthesis of published data.

The review highlights that extremophiles possess distinct physiological and biochemical traits that make them promising platforms for resource recovery and bioprospecting. Their stress‑adaptation mechanisms and unique metabolic pathways could be harnessed for applications aligned with clean water, clean energy and land‑based solutions.

Understanding and exploiting these traits may open new avenues for sustainable biotechnologies that turn harsh environments into sources of valuable products.
picks.why: These hardy microbes could be turned into green factories for water treatment, renewable fuels, or land‑based bio‑products.

picks.title: Marine Microalgal Genes: Unlocking a New Era of Sustainable High Value PUFA Production for Neuroprotective Applications.
picks.hook: New microalgal genes boost sustainable PUFA yields for neuroprotective supplements.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to examine how genes from marine microalgae could be used to create sustainable, high‑value sources of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) that protect the brain. The authors surveyed the genetic pathways that enable these tiny sea plants to make important omega‑3 and omega‑6 fats such as eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). By reviewing the current knowledge of these genes and the biotechnological tools available, they highlighted both the promise and the challenges of engineering algae for reliable PUFA production.

The review focused on marine microalgae, which naturally synthesize large amounts of EPA and DHA, and discussed how modern genetic techniques could tap into this capacity. It compared different gene candidates, metabolic engineering strategies, and cultivation approaches, drawing on recent experimental reports.

The authors concluded that marine microalgal genes represent a compelling resource for developing new, dependable production systems for neuroprotective PUFAs, but that further work is needed to overcome technical and economic hurdles.

Understanding these genetic tools is important because they could enable greener, more consistent supplies of essential fatty acids that support brain health.
picks.why: Harnessing algae genes could provide a sustainable source of brain‑protective omega‑3 fats for food and health products.

picks.title: Low-temperature plasma technology: comprehensive applications in microalgae cultivation, mutagenesis, and downstream processing.
picks.hook: Low‑temperature plasma enhances algal growth, mutation rates, and downstream processing.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to explore how low‑temperature plasma (LTP) technologies could improve microalgae cultivation, mutation and downstream processing. The authors reviewed the effects of both atmospheric and room‑temperature plasma on microalgae, focusing on how plasma dose influences outcomes.

They examined existing research on LTP applied to microalgae, looking at laboratory‑scale experiments that used plasma generators to treat algal cultures during growth, to induce genetic changes, and to assist in harvesting or product extraction.

The review found that LTP can act as a versatile tool, enhancing strain performance and reducing processing costs, with effects that depend on the amount of plasma applied.

Understanding these plasma‑algae interactions could help develop more efficient and affordable algae‑based products for fuels, nutrition, and environmental applications.
picks.why: Plasma‑enhanced algae processes may lower costs and boost yields, making algal fuels and nutrients more accessible.

picks.title: Strong static magnetic field enhances biomass and high-value lipid production in Chlorella pyrenoidosa via metabolic regulation.
picks.hook: Static magnetic fields trigger metabolic shifts, raising Chlorella lipid output for fuels.
picks.article:
A recent study examined whether a strong static magnetic field could boost growth and valuable oil production in the microalga Chlorella pyrenoidosa. The researchers grew the algae under normal light while exposing them to a magnetic field of 3 T for 10 minutes, then measured biomass and lipid output.

The magnetic treatment proved optimal, leading to a biomass of 1.25 g L⁻¹, which the authors note is a 42 % increase over the control culture. Moreover, the overall biomass productivity rose 1.82‑fold to 0.31 g L⁻¹ day⁻¹.

These results suggest that applying a brief, strong magnetic field can re‑program algal metabolism to yield more cells and potentially more high‑value lipids, offering a simple physical tool for improving algal bioprocesses.
picks.why: Magnetic enhancement could raise algae yields without extra nutrients, making bio‑fuel and nutraceutical production more efficient.

picks.title: The genomic origins of cyanobacterial morphological diversity.
picks.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
picks.hook: Study maps genomic roots of cyanobacterial shape diversity, shedding light on evolution.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to uncover the genetic basis for the wide range of shapes and structures seen in cyanobacteria, the only prokaryotes that perform oxygenic photosynthesis.

The researchers examined cyanobacterial genomes, focusing on genes linked to filamentous growth and the differentiation of specialized cells, to trace how these traits evolved.

They found that the genomic mechanisms driving repeated transitions between single‑cell and multicellular forms remain unresolved, highlighting gaps in our understanding of cyanobacterial morphological evolution.

Understanding these genetic switches is important because it sheds light on how early oxygen‑producing microbes diversified, a process that shaped Earth's ecosystems.
picks.why: Deciphering cyanobacterial shape control can inform algae engineering for sustainable bio‑production.
